newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan stocks dive on Wall Street spillover effect. [CORRECTED 07:19 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Japan stocks dive on Wall Street spillover effect. [CORRECTED 07:19 GMT]

text.p: Japan stocks tumbled more than two percent in choppy morning trade on Friday on what traders said was a spillover effect from Wall Street's second largest points fall on Monday (corrects day from Friday to Monday). The dollar, meanwhile, dipped in mid-morning Tokyo trade on renewed jitters over Japan's swelling trade surplus, although the figures announced for the surplus in July showed lower-than-expected growth.

The plunge in the Dow Industrials on Friday worsened sentiment on a Tokyo stock market already bearish due to Japan's weak economic recovery, traders said. The Dow lost 247.37 points to 7,694.66, its second-biggest point drop ever.
The Tokyo stock market's benchmark 225-share Nikkei average shed 391.74 points, or 2.03 percent, to 18,934.29 by midday. It briefly fell as low as 18,835.48.
Its September futures were down 520 points at 18,920 by midday.

Wall Street's plunge hit shares of leading Japanese high-tech firms, which had recently been buoyed by the stellar performance of U.S. high-tech shares and by their own strong exports to the United States.

"The focus will be on what will happen to the New York market next, but I expect its correction to be just a technical one," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd. "So far, New York's impact on Tokyo has been limited to high-tech shares."
Turnover remained modest at 189 million shares by midday on the first section of the Tokyo bourse as many participants were still away on summer holidays.
"The Japanese market is currently vulnerable to negative news because of the shaky recovery in the domestic economy," said Keiko Kondo, a strategist at Merrill Lynch Japan Inc.
She said New York's losses would have a limited impact on Tokyo, but added: "For the Nikkei 225 to head higher, the sentiment towards the (Japanese) economy has to improve."
The dollar slipped against the yen in Tokyo morning trade to around 117.00 yen from its New York close of around 117.40 on renewed jitters over Japan's rising trade surplus.
The currency's losses came after Deputy U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) Jeffrey Lang told Reuters in Tokyo that the United States was concerned about Japan's trade figures.

Asked how concerned the USTR was by the nearly 70 percent rise in Japan's overall July trade surplus and the 35 percent rise in its surplus with the United States announced earlier on Monday, Lang said, "I haven't seen the trade figures this morning, but we are concerned."
Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus rose 69.7 percent in July from a year earlier, another hefty jump, but the rise was at the lower end of economists' forecasts.
The overall surplus came in at 849.08 billion yen ($7.25 billion), while the surplus with the United States grew 35.7 percent to 420.55 billion yen ($3.59 billion).
On the Japanese bond market, the key September 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) futures contract ended the morning firmer, but was off its session high.

The market initially rallied on falls in Tokyo stocks but later fizzled amid the summer holiday lull. Wall Street's dive had a limited impact on JGBs as short-end U.S. Treasuries firmed due to a flight to quality by investors, traders said.
The September contract was up 0.08 at 126.91 at midday. It rose as high as 127.05 after opening at 127.00. ($1=117 yen)
